meta.blurb: In 1930 Gandhi walked nearly four hundred kilometres to the sea to pick up a handful of salt, and mass protest followed. Why? Follow salt from desert caravans and Roman roads to hated taxes, and see how it shaped wars and freedom.

B1B2: A pinch of salt seems like the smallest thing in the kitchen. Yet for thousands of years it has built cities, moved caravans and started wars.
The human body needs a small amount of salt to work properly. We lose some of it in sweat and tears, so we must replace it from the food we eat.
Salt can be found in four main places: the sea, salt lakes, underground rock and salty springs. Long ago, ancient seas dried up and left thick layers of salt buried deep in the earth.
Deer, cattle and other animals will travel a long way to reach a salt lick, a patch of salty earth. Early hunters probably followed the animals, and so they found these places too.
Early farmers ate mostly grain and vegetables, which hold very little salt. Many scholars think this is why farming peoples began adding salt to their meals and trading for it.
Salt draws water out of food, and without water the germs that make food rot cannot grow. That is why people used it to keep fish, meat, olives and cheese for months.
In warm places, people led seawater into shallow ponds and let the sun and wind dry it. What remained was a crust of white salt, which workers raked into heaps.
Where the sun was weak, salt makers boiled salty water in large clay pots or metal pans. This used up a great deal of wood or coal, and whole forests were sometimes cut down to feed the fires.

In Sichuan, in western China, workers drilled deep wells to reach salty water underground. They used bamboo cables and iron bits, and by the nineteenth century some wells were more than a thousand metres deep.
Chinese rulers saw that everyone had to buy salt, so they took control of its sale. For many centuries, the money from this tax helped to pay for armies, roads and canals.
The ancient Egyptians preserved their dead with natron, a salty mineral collected from dry lake beds. They also preserved fish with salt, which was an important food for ordinary people.
In the Austrian Alps, miners at Hallstatt dug salt out of the mountain for more than three thousand years. The salt made the people there rich, and they traded it across much of Europe.

The word salary may come from the Latin word for salt, and salad means something that has been salted. Salzburg in Austria, and English towns such as Nantwich and Droitwich, have names that point to salt.
Near the mouth of the Tiber, the Romans ran salt pans, and a road called the Via Salaria carried the salt inland. Its name means the Salt Road, and some of it can still be followed today.
In Roman ports, workers packed fish and salt together in large tanks and left them in the sun. The result was garum, a strong fish sauce that cooks used all over the empire.
In parts of Ethiopia, flat bars of salt served as money until well into the twentieth century. These bars, called amole, were carried by traders and exchanged for food, cloth and other goods.
For many centuries, camel caravans crossed the Sahara desert carrying salt to West Africa. On the way back, they carried gold, ivory and other valuable goods north.
In 1352, the traveller Ibn Battuta visited Taghaza, a desert town where the houses were built of salt blocks. He wrote that it was a miserable place, with no trees, only sand and a mine of salt.

In the Danakil Depression in Ethiopia, one of the hottest places on Earth, Afar workers still cut salt from the ground. Camel trains carry the blocks to markets in the highlands, just as they did long ago.
The peoples of the Americas were making salt long before any Europeans arrived. At Maras, in Peru, thousands of small pools still fill with salty spring water that the sun dries into salt.
In many countries of Eastern Europe, an honoured guest is welcomed with bread and salt. In other parts of the world, people who have shared salt are bound by friendship and must not harm each other.
In medieval Europe, salt moved along old trade routes that were often called salt roads. One of them, the Old Salt Road, ran from the salt town of Luneburg to the Baltic port of Lubeck.

In the Baltic and North seas, fishermen caught huge numbers of herring, and workers packed them in barrels with salt. Merchants of the Hanseatic League, a group of trading towns, sold the fish across northern Europe.
Venice, a city built on islands in a lagoon, made and sold salt from very early times. Salt from its own pans, and later from other lands, helped to make the city rich and powerful.
At Wieliczka, near Krakow in Poland, miners dug for salt for more than seven hundred years. Deep underground, they carved chapels with statues and even chandeliers made of salt.
In the North Atlantic, fishermen caught huge numbers of cod and packed them in salt. Salted cod could last for many months, so it became a cheap food for people across Europe.

In Cheshire, in the northwest of England, three towns are called Nantwich, Northwich and Middlewich. The word wich was used for a place where salt was made, and these towns grew up around salty springs.
In France, the king taxed salt, and this tax was called the gabelle. It was hated, because some regions paid much more than others, and families had to buy a fixed amount.

Where salt was taxed heavily, smugglers carried it secretly across borders at night. In France they were called faux-sauniers, and those caught could be sent to prison or to the royal ships as rowers.
In 1648 the Russian government raised the tax on salt, and the people of Moscow rose in anger. The Salt Riot became so serious that the young tsar sent away his chief minister and changed the tax.
Salt does more than stop food from rotting, because it also guides the helpful bacteria that make food tasty. Cheese, pickles, olives and soy sauce all depend on salt in some way.

Ships on long voyages could not carry fresh meat, so sailors ate beef and pork preserved in barrels of salt. Without salt, the great sea voyages of exploration and trade would have been very difficult.

Salt works were hot, dangerous places, and in many times and countries they relied on prisoners or enslaved people. On the Turks Islands in the Caribbean, for example, enslaved workers raked salt under the burning sun.

Armies needed salt to feed their soldiers, so salt works became important targets in war. In the American Civil War, the North tried to cut off the South's salt, and Saltville in Virginia was attacked twice.
At Syracuse, in New York State, salty springs had long been used to make salt. When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, boats could carry the salt far away, and Syracuse became known as the Salt City.
In the nineteenth century, chemists found ways to turn salt into other useful substances. Soda ash and chlorine, for example, were needed to make soap, glass, paper and cloth.

In the late nineteenth century, canning, ice-making machines and refrigerated ships let people keep food fresh without salt. Salt was no longer the only way to protect a harvest, and its great power began to fade.

In some places, especially in mountains, food contains too little iodine, a nutrient that the body needs. In the 1920s, Switzerland and the United States began adding iodine to table salt, and illness from the lack of it fell.
Today, many people eat more salt than their bodies need, and much of it comes from packaged foods. Health experts link too much salt with high blood pressure, and they advise most people to eat less.
When Britain ruled India, the government made salt expensive by adding a heavy tax. To stop smuggling, it grew a great thorny hedge across the country, thousands of kilometres long, and guarded it.

In March 1930, Mohandas Gandhi, a leader of India's movement for independence, set out on foot from his home near Ahmedabad. He and his followers walked for twenty-four days to reach the sea, where he planned to break the salt law.

On 6 April 1930, Gandhi reached the beach at Dandi and picked up a handful of salty mud. People across India copied him, and the British arrested tens of thousands of protesters, including Gandhi himself.
Today, the world produces hundreds of millions of tonnes of salt every year. It comes from sea-water ponds, from underground mines and from brine that is evaporated by machines.
Much of the salt that people use today never reaches the kitchen at all. In cold countries, trucks spread it on icy roads in winter, because salt makes ice melt at lower temperatures.

In Bolivia, the Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world, a white plain stretching to the horizon. Beneath its surface, the salty water also holds lithium, a metal that is used in batteries for phones and cars.
Many cultures have used salt in their rituals and in their sayings. In Japan, sumo wrestlers throw salt into the ring to purify it, and the Hebrew Bible speaks of a covenant of salt.
Rulers in many different parts of the world taxed salt for very similar reasons. Everyone needed it, it came from a small number of places, and nobody could easily do without it.
Salt lost much of its power because it became cheap and easy to find. Railways, steamships and modern mining moved it quickly to markets and brought the price down.
The salt in your shaker may have lain underground for millions of years, in the bed of an ancient sea. Workers dug it up or dried it from seawater, and then trucks and ships carried it to a shop.
Salt helped to shape roads and cities, to pay for armies and to start protests. The next time you pick up the salt shaker, remember how much history is inside it.
C1C2: A grain of salt is so small that we hardly notice it, and so common that most of us never wonder where it comes from. Yet for thousands of years this humble mineral has decided where cities were built, which roads were travelled and which governments grew rich. This book follows its trail around the world, from ancient pans beside the sea to the salt shaker on your table.

Salt is made of two elements, sodium and chloride, and the human body depends on both of them to carry nerve signals, move muscles and balance the water in its cells. We lose a little salt every day through sweat and other fluids, and the body cannot make any to replace it. That simple fact explains why people everywhere, in every age, have gone to such lengths to find it.

Salt is found in four main places: the oceans, the shallow lakes of dry regions, springs of salty water called brines, and solid beds of rock salt underground. Those buried beds are the remains of ancient seas that evaporated millions of years ago, leaving layers of salt that were later covered by sand and clay. Different peoples learned to use each of these sources, and the method they chose shaped how they lived.

Animals have always known where to find salt, and herds of deer, cattle and bison will beat paths through the forest to reach a salty spring or a patch of mineral earth. Hunters who followed them probably discovered these places long before anyone thought of mining, and some old tracks may have begun as routes to a lick. Many hunters also got enough salt from the meat and blood of the animals they ate, so they did not need to add any.

When people settled down to farm, their meals changed from meat to bread, porridge and vegetables, foods that contain very little of the salt the body needs. Many scholars think this change created a steady demand for salt, because a farmer could grow grain but could not grow salt in his field. From that moment, salt was something that had to be fetched, bought or traded from somewhere else.

Salt keeps food by drawing out the moisture on which bacteria and moulds depend, and a fish or a joint of meat that has been packed in it can stay edible for months or even years. Before refrigerators, this was the only reliable way to carry a harvest or a catch through the winter, or across an ocean. Whoever controlled the salt therefore controlled the food supply, and that gave salt a power that no spice or jewel could match.

Along sunny coasts from the Mediterranean to India, people learned to channel seawater into a series of shallow ponds and leave it to the sun and the wind. As the water evaporated, the brine grew stronger, and at last a crust of white crystals formed on the bottom, ready to be raked into heaps. The method needed almost no fuel and little equipment, and in some places it is still used in much the same way today.

In rainy or cold countries, where the sun could not do the work, salt makers boiled brine from springs and wells in clay pots and later in large iron pans. The process swallowed fuel at an astonishing rate, and entire forests were sometimes felled to keep the fires burning beneath the salt works. Archaeologists have found traces of such boiling in China, Europe and Africa that go back several thousand years.

In Sichuan, in western China, drillers invented a way of sinking narrow wells by lifting and dropping a heavy iron bit on a bamboo cable, and over many centuries they reached astonishing depths. By the nineteenth century, some of their wells were more than a thousand metres deep, and the brine was sometimes boiled with natural gas that rose from the same holes. It was one of the great engineering achievements of the premodern world, and it was done with bamboo, iron and human muscle.

Chinese governments realised very early that salt was a product no household could do without, and that a tax on it would raise money without the need to count anyone's land or income. From the Han dynasty onwards, officials often ran the salt trade as a state monopoly, and for long periods it brought in a large share of the empire's revenue. The same system, however, encouraged smuggling, corruption and fierce quarrels over who should profit.

To make a mummy, the ancient Egyptians covered the body with natron, a naturally occurring mixture of salts collected from dry lake beds, which drew out the moisture and kept the flesh from rotting. The same principle was used on a humbler scale in the kitchen, where fish from the Nile and the marshes were cleaned, salted and dried for ordinary families. Salt, in other words, was already protecting both the dead and the living more than four thousand years ago.

High in the Austrian Alps, miners at Hallstatt cut tunnels deep into the mountain and hacked out blocks of rock salt for more than three thousand years, carrying them out in leather bags and wooden frames. Salt preserved the bodies, clothes and tools of some of the miners so well that archaeologists can study them today almost as if they had been lost yesterday. The wealth that flowed from the mine made Hallstatt a centre of trade, and its name has been given to a whole early European culture.

Salt has left its mark on language, and the English word salary probably comes from the Latin salarium, which some ancient writers linked to an allowance of salt, although scholars debate the exact connection. Salad means something that has been salted, and place names such as Salzburg in Austria and Droitwich in England record the places where salt was made. Even our common praise for an honest worker, that he is worth his salt, points back to the time when the mineral had a real price.

Rome was supplied by salt pans near the mouth of the River Tiber, and the Via Salaria, whose name means the Salt Road, carried the white crystals inland to the hill towns and into the heart of the city. The Romans valued salt so highly that the state sometimes regulated its sale, and the government treated it as a matter of public concern. A track that began as a salt route had become, by the time of the empire, one of the busy highways of Italy.

Along the coasts of the Mediterranean, Roman workers packed fish and salt into stone tanks and left them to ferment in the sun, producing garum, a pungent sauce that was bottled in clay jars and shipped across the empire. Rich households and poor ones alike used it to season their food, and the best varieties cost a great deal of money. None of this would have been possible without cheap salt in huge quantities, which the empire's pans and mines supplied.

In many parts of the world salt itself served as a kind of money, because it was valuable, easy to divide and wanted by everyone. In the highlands of Ethiopia, flat bars of salt called amole were used in markets until the twentieth century, and travellers carried them like coins to pay for food and lodging. Such customs show how a plain mineral could stand in for money wherever coins were scarce.

For more than a thousand years, camel caravans of hundreds or even thousands of animals crossed the Sahara carrying slabs of salt from desert mines to the towns and villages of West Africa, where salt was scarce. They returned with gold, ivory and other goods that were wanted on the shores of the Mediterranean. Whole kingdoms, such as the empire of Mali, grew powerful by taxing and protecting this exchange.

In the fourteenth century the great Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta crossed the Sahara and stopped at Taghaza, a settlement where the houses and even the mosque were built from slabs of rock salt and roofed with camel skins. He found it an unpleasant place, with no trees and bad water, where the miners lived by cutting salt and sending it south. From Taghaza the slabs travelled to Timbuktu and other markets, where they were exchanged for the gold of the Sahel.

In the Danakil Depression of northern Ethiopia, one of the hottest and lowest places on Earth, Afar workers still cut slabs of salt from the dried lake bed with simple tools, shaping them into rectangular blocks. Camel trains then carry the blocks up to the highland markets, in a journey that has changed little in hundreds of years, although trucks now take a share of the trade. The work is hard and the heat is punishing, but it remains a living for many families.

The peoples of the Americas were making salt long before any European arrived, whether by boiling brine, as the Maya did on the coast of Mexico, or by gathering the crust that formed on shallow lakes. At Maras, in the Peruvian Andes, a salty spring feeds thousands of small terraced pools that have been used for centuries, and families still harvest salt there by hand. Salt was a trade good of the first importance across both continents, linking the highlands to the coast.

In Russia, Ukraine and many neighbouring lands, an honoured guest is still welcomed with a loaf of bread and a small dish of salt, a custom that expresses the wish that the visitor will never go hungry. In several other cultures, an old saying holds that those who have eaten salt together owe each other loyalty and protection. Because salt was precious and belonged on every table, it became a natural symbol of friendship, trust and promises.

In the Middle Ages, a network of trade routes known as salt roads crossed Europe, and the best known of them, the Old Salt Road, led from the brine springs of Luneburg to the Baltic port of Lubeck. Carts, pack horses and barges carried the salt along such routes, and towns that stood on them collected tolls and grew prosperous. The wealth that flowed along these roads helped to pay for the churches, town halls and merchants' houses that still stand there.

Herring swam in vast shoals through the Baltic and the North Sea, and once they were gutted and packed in barrels with salt, they could be carried hundreds of kilometres inland to feed people who had never seen the sea. Merchants of the Hanseatic League, a powerful alliance of trading towns around the northern seas, made a fortune from this trade and took good care to control the salt supply on which it depended. Fish on Fridays and in Lent, which the Church required, kept the demand strong.

Venice, built on islands in a lagoon, had salt pans around its edges almost from the beginning, and by the later Middle Ages its merchants were importing salt from distant shores and selling it all over northern Italy. The government treated the trade as a source of revenue and a tool of diplomacy, and neighbouring cities often found that their supplies depended on Venetian goodwill. Salt, along with spices and glass, was one of the foundations of the republic's long prosperity.

The mine at Wieliczka, near Krakow in southern Poland, was worked from the thirteenth century and for hundreds of years provided a large share of the Polish crown's income. Over the generations the miners carved vast chambers and chapels out of the grey rock salt, adding altars, statues and chandeliers whose crystal pendants are also made of salt. Today the mine is one of the most visited historic sites in all of Poland.

From about the year 1500, European fishermen, among them the Basques, followed the cod across the North Atlantic, and on the shores of Newfoundland they dried and salted enormous catches that fed millions of people across the ocean. The fish could be stored for a year or more, so it was a dependable food for ships, towns and armies, and for Catholics on days when meat was forbidden. Few foods have done more to knit the two sides of the Atlantic together.

In Cheshire, in the northwest of England, the ending wich on the names of Nantwich, Northwich and Middlewich tells us that salt was being made there, probably from Roman times and certainly from the Middle Ages. Brine was pumped up from underground and boiled in great pans, and by the nineteenth century Cheshire salt was being shipped to the whole world. The ground in some of the towns even sank, as the salt was removed from beneath the houses.

The French salt tax, known as the gabelle, became one of the most hated burdens in the kingdom, because the rate varied enormously between provinces and households had to buy a fixed amount each year, needed or not. A pound of salt that cost a few coins in one region might cost many times as much in the next, which encouraged a flourishing trade in smuggling. The gabelle was abolished in 1790, during the French Revolution, although a salt tax returned under Napoleon.

The temptation to avoid a heavy salt tax produced armies of smugglers, who carried bags of untaxed salt across provincial borders at night, often by quiet paths and in small groups. If they were caught, the penalties could be severe, and many smugglers were sent to prison or condemned to serve as rowers on the king's ships. Whole families lived on this dangerous trade, and many ordinary people sympathised with the smugglers rather than the tax collectors.

In 1648 the Russian government, short of money, raised the price of salt by means of a new tax, and the people of Moscow answered with a violent uprising that became known as the Salt Riot. The crowd attacked the houses of unpopular officials, and the young tsar was forced to send his chief minister out of the city and to change the tax. It was one of many occasions in history when an increase in the price of a basic necessity caused a ruler to fear for his throne.

Salt does more than hold back decay, for in the right amount it holds back harmful organisms while allowing helpful ones to thrive, and in this way it makes possible some of the world's best-loved foods. Cheese, sauerkraut, kimchi, miso and soy sauce all depend on salt for their texture and flavour, as do cured hams and sausages from Spain to China. A cuisine without salt would be a cuisine without a large part of its tradition.

Before canning and refrigeration, a ship could carry fresh meat only as long as it lasted, so navies and merchant fleets loaded their holds with barrels of beef and pork that had been packed in salt. The meat became hard and very salty, and sailors had to soak it before it could be eaten, but it did not spoil in the heat of the tropics. In this unglamorous way, salt made possible the long voyages that connected the continents.

Behind the story of salt lies a story of hard labour, for evaporating ponds and mines were hot, dangerous and unhealthy, and in many societies the work was done by prisoners, enslaved people or poorly paid peasants. On the Turks Islands in the Caribbean, enslaved Africans raked salt in the burning sun, standing for hours in brine that damaged their skin. The wealth that salt created was, in other words, often paid for by people who shared very little of it.

Armies of the past marched on meat that had been preserved in salt, and a shortage could be as dangerous as a lack of gunpowder. During the American Revolution, salt was so scarce that it was rationed in many places, and during the Civil War the Union blockaded the Southern coast and attacked the great salt works at Saltville, Virginia, in 1864. The Confederacy never fully solved its salt problem, and its soldiers and civilians felt the shortage for years.

Near the shores of Onondaga Lake, in what is now Syracuse, New York, springs of strong brine had long been used by the Onondaga people and later by settlers to make salt. When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, boats could carry barrels of salt cheaply to the Great Lakes and the Hudson River, and the town grew into a busy industrial centre known as the Salt City. The canal and the salt business fed each other, and together they helped to open the American interior to settlement.

In the nineteenth century, industrial chemists learned to split salt into its parts, and the substances they made, such as soda ash and chlorine, became essential raw materials for soap, glass, paper, textiles and many other products. The Leblanc process and later the Solvay process turned salt from a food into the foundation of a great chemical industry, and factories were built beside salt fields to feed it. Today most of the world's salt is used by industry rather than eaten at the table.

With the arrival of canning, mechanical refrigeration and refrigerated railway wagons and ships in the later nineteenth century, food could at last be kept fresh without salt. The old fear of a winter without preserved food faded, and the mineral that had once decided the fate of cities became an ordinary item in the shop. Even so, we still salt bacon, ham and fish today, now for taste and tradition rather than necessity.

In regions far from the sea, and especially in mountain valleys, the soil often contains little iodine, and people who lived on local food could develop goitre, a swelling of the neck, and their children's development could be harmed. In the 1920s, Switzerland and the United States began adding small amounts of iodine to table salt, and the idea soon spread to most of the world. It has been called one of the cheapest and most successful public health measures ever introduced.

Where salt was once scarce, it is now abundant, and in many countries people eat considerably more than the body requires, much of it hidden in bread, processed meals and snacks. Large studies link a high salt intake with raised blood pressure, which is a risk factor for heart disease and strokes, and health authorities therefore recommend limiting it. How much any one person should eat is a question for a doctor, since needs and risks differ from person to person.

Under British rule in India, salt could be produced and sold only under government control, and a heavy tax made it expensive for the poorest families, who needed it most because they worked in the heat and ate simple food. To stop smuggling between regions, officials created a customs line, partly made of a dense thorny hedge, that stretched for thousands of kilometres across the subcontinent and was patrolled by thousands of guards. The salt tax would later become a powerful and lasting symbol of foreign rule.

On 12 March 1930, Mohandas Gandhi, the leader of India's movement for independence, left his ashram near Ahmedabad with about eighty followers and set out on foot toward the sea, nearly four hundred kilometres away. Along the way, the crowd of walkers grew, villagers came out to cheer, and newspapers around the world reported the progress of the march. His goal was simple and deliberate, which was to defy the salt law by making salt from seawater with his own hands.

On the morning of 6 April 1930, Gandhi bent down on the beach at Dandi and picked up a handful of salty mud, an act of open defiance against the salt law. Across India, people began to make their own salt in protest, and tens of thousands were arrested, including Gandhi himself, but the campaign drew the attention of the world to the demand for independence. India became free in 1947, and the salt tax, which had seemed so ordinary, had been one of the issues that turned millions of people against the old order.

Modern salt production exceeds two hundred million tonnes a year, and it comes from three main sources, which are solar ponds, underground mines, and brine wells whose liquid is boiled down in closed vacuum pans. The largest producers include China, the United States, India and Germany, together making up a large part of the total. Compared with the days of caravans and monopolies, salt has become astonishingly cheap and plentiful.

A surprising share of modern salt is spread on roads, where it lowers the freezing point of water and keeps highways open through the winter in places such as Canada, northern Europe and the northern United States. The benefits for safety are clear, but the salty water that runs off the roads can harm rivers, soil and wildlife, so engineers are experimenting with more careful ways of using it. Even in this humble role, the old mineral shapes the way that we live.

The Salar de Uyuni, high in the Bolivian Andes, covers more than ten thousand square kilometres and is the largest salt flat on Earth, a dazzling white plain that mirrors the sky after rain. Beneath the crust lies brine rich in lithium, the metal used in the batteries of phones and electric cars, and countries from Bolivia to Chile and Argentina are now competing to develop such resources. Salt lakes, which once supplied the kitchen, may now help to power the world.

Because salt preserved and cleansed, many traditions have treated it as a symbol of purity, loyalty and lasting agreements. In Japan, sumo wrestlers scatter handfuls of salt in the ring before a bout to purify it, and the Hebrew Bible speaks of a covenant of salt to describe a promise that will not spoil. Such customs, found in very different parts of the world, show how deeply a simple mineral can settle into human imagination.

Rulers in many parts of the world were drawn to the salt tax by the same logic, since everyone needed salt, it came from a few known places where officials could watch it, and no household could easily go without. A tax of this kind raised large sums quietly and steadily, but it fell hardest on the poor, who spent a bigger share of their income on basic goods. That is why salt taxes so often stirred up anger, and why some of history's biggest protests began over a pinch of salt.

Salt lost its political power gradually, as railways, steamships and modern mining machinery made it possible to move huge quantities cheaply to every corner of a country. When the price fell, the taxes that had once raised fortunes were hardly worth collecting, and one government after another abolished them. A substance that had been guarded by armies and governed by monopolies was now sold in plain paper packets for a few coins.

The salt in your kitchen may have lain buried for millions of years in the bed of a vanished sea, or it may have been dried this summer from the water of a living one. Either way, it has passed through the hands of miners or pond workers, through factories and ships, and across a shop counter before reaching your table. Behind every pinch lies a long chain of work that most of us never see.

Salt marked out the roads of ancient Rome, enriched the kingdoms of Africa, filled the treasuries of emperors and kings, and in the end gave a movement for freedom its most memorable symbol. Its story reminds us that the greatest forces in history are often hidden in the most ordinary things, and that a humble commodity can carry great power. The next time you reach for the shaker at the table, you will be holding a little of that story in your hand.
